title: REST API
short: Name things with URLs, act on them with HTTP verbs.
what: REST is the most common way to shape a web API. Each thing (a pet, an order) gets a URL, and you act on it with the standard HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH or PUT changes, DELETE removes. Each request carries everything the server needs, so any server can answer it.
analogy: A library. Every book has a shelf number, and there are only a few actions: borrow, return, renew. Nobody invents a new counter for each book.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: A pet shelter's API. The URL /pets names a collection (a noun). GET reads it. The answer 200 means OK, here are 3 pets.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: POST /pets with {name: Rex} in the body creates a pet. The server answers 201 Created and the new id, 7.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: GET /pets/7 reads that one pet. The server keeps no memory of you between requests, so any of its copies can answer.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: PATCH /pets/7 changes only the fields you send, here the age. PUT would replace the whole pet with what you send.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: DELETE /pets/7 removes it. 204 means done, and there is nothing to send back.

frames.label: request -> response
frames.say: Ask for pet 7 again: 404. Codes in the 400s mean the request was wrong; 500s mean the server broke.

when: Clients create, read, update and delete records
Web, phone and partner apps share one backend
output:
POST /pets -> 201 7
GET /pets/7 -> 200 {'name': 'Rex'}
DELETE /pets/7 -> 204 (no body)
GET /pets/7 -> 404 not found
cost: 1 round trip, O(1) with an index
watch: Put nouns in URLs and let the method be the verb: /pets/7, not /getPet?id=7.
GET must never change data. Browsers, caches and retries repeat GETs freely.
Return long lists in pages (?limit=20&cursor=...), never all at once.
